items.text: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties

segments.text: Treaty law explains how international agreements are made, interpreted, applied, amended, invalidated and terminated.

Use the Vienna Convention as the map: conclusion and consent to be bound, reservations, entry into force, pacta sunt servanda, interpretation, third states, invalidity, termination/suspension and consequences.
Primary international authority: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969, especially Articles 26 and 31–32 for performance and interpretation.

The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 provides the standard framework for treaties between states. The life-cycle begins with negotiation and adoption of text, moves through authentication and consent to be bound, and then to entry into force, performance, interpretation, amendment and possible suspension or termination.

Consent to be bound may be expressed by signature, ratification, acceptance, approval, accession or another agreed method depending on the treaty. The legal consequence of signature alone therefore depends on the treaty and the applicable rules.

Pacta sunt servanda, reflected in Article 26 of the Convention, means that every treaty in force is binding on its parties and must be performed in good faith. A party may not simply invoke internal-law difficulty as a general excuse for non-performance.

A reservation is a unilateral statement by which a state seeks to exclude or modify the legal effect of certain treaty provisions in their application to that state. Reservations are controlled by the treaty and the Convention framework, including compatibility with the treaty's object and purpose where the treaty does not resolve the matter differently.
Treaties generally do not create obligations or rights for third states without the conditions required by treaty law. This reflects the consensual structure of treaty obligation.

Article 31 begins interpretation with the ordinary meaning of terms in their context and in light of the treaty's object and purpose, applied in good faith. Supplementary means under Article 32 may assist in the circumstances provided by the Convention. Interpretation is therefore a legal method, not an invitation to choose any policy-preferred meaning.

Invalidity and termination must remain separate. Invalidity concerns defects affecting consent or the legal validity of the treaty, such as specified error, fraud, coercion or conflict with a peremptory norm. Termination concerns ending or suspending obligations under a treaty that was validly in force, for example under treaty provisions or legally recognized grounds.

items.text: Treaty law can be learned as a life-cycle:
negotiation and adoption; signature or other authentication; consent to be bound; entry into force; performance; interpretation; amendment; and possible suspension or termination.
Pacta sunt servanda expresses the basic principle that treaties in force must be performed in good faith. Domestic inconvenience does not by itself cancel an international obligation.

Reservations allow a state, within applicable rules, to seek exclusion or modification of the legal effect of certain treaty provisions in relation to that state. Their permissibility depends on the treaty and compatibility rules.

Interpretation starts with the ordinary meaning of treaty terms in their context and in light of the treaty's object and purpose. It is a disciplined legal method, not a search for any politically convenient meaning.
Invalidity concerns defects affecting the treaty or consent; termination concerns bringing obligations to an end after a valid treaty exists. Keep these concepts separate.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not use “treaty is invalid” and “treaty has terminated” as interchangeable expressions. They answer different legal questions.

segments.text: Pacta sunt servanda means treaties in force bind parties and must be performed in good faith.
Reservation rules depend on the treaty and compatibility with its object and purpose.
Treaty interpretation is structured, not free-form.
